newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: New Yugo farm policy needed for better funding.
newsitem.headline: New Yugo farm policy needed for better funding.

text.p: Yugoslavia needs to create a new agriculture policy and secure stable sources of finance for the industry which helped the country out of nearly four years of economic sanctions, a government official said on Wednesday.
"Agriculture deserves much better treatment than the one it enjoys," Yugoslav deputy Agriculture Minister Milan Prostran told a bankers meeting.

Prostran said the industry had become completely exhausted over the last six years, having lost around $5 billion during years of sanctions when funds were directed to other sectors of the economy and financial support was generally inadequate.
A possible solution was a completely new government agriculture policy, he said.
"The state must also create a special fund for agriculture rehabilitation and financing. If not, problems will worsen," he added.
Yugoslavia has become increasingly reliant on its agriculture, which together with the food processing industry accounted for around 30 percent of its gross domestic product (GDP) in 1996.
In the past, agriculture took up only eight percent of GDP.

After experiencing the worst wheat harvest in 25 years and declining maize output due to a smaller area under those crops and bad weather in 1996, the government looked determined to improve the poor record.

A 930 million dinar ($166.8 million) Serbian agriculture budget was not seen supporting the commitment. But Serbia was determined to gather funds from the National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY), commercial banks and trading firms.
Industry analysts said around 1.2 billion dinars would be needed for spring sowing and commercial banks were expected to provide almost 30 percent of the required funds.

Nearly 900 million dinars should come from the NBY in the form of special purpose funds and additional credits, from commercial banks and partly from the 15 percent reserve requirement they set aside with the NBY, as well as trading companies and food processors.
But banks pressed by growing illiquidity said they would not be able to meet the request.

"Banks do not have funds for that purpose. In fact, there are no dinars to be transformed into long-term borrowing. Yugoslav banks dispose only of short-term money," said general manager of Vojvodjanska banka Zivota Mihajlovic.
Mihajlovic, also chairing the Yugoslav Chamber of Commerce Banking Committee, said more debt rescheduling and fresh credits to agriculture would not solve the problem.
"A solution should be sought in changing the position of agriculture in the Yugoslav economy," he said.

Bankers said agriculture producers could not afford to pay the old debt, let alone incur new . They suggested the NBY should create a special purpose reserve account and drain funds from those banks which did not finance agriculture.
Meanwhile, the Serbian government 's earlier attempts to raise funds by issuing forward contracts selling agricultural produce as collateral have proved futile.

Out of 437.5 million dinars in contracts issued by the Serbian Commodity Reserve Agency only 84 million have been sold via the Belgrade bourse to date. The only buyers have been flour mills. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
